result:
The morning light filters through the leaves like liquid gold, and for a moment the entire forest seems to hold its breath. I’ve always been fascinated by thresholds—those delicate spaces between one state and another. Dawn is one. The surface of a lake is another. A sentence right before it becomes a story.

There’s something quietly rebellious about paying attention. In a world engineered to harvest our focus, choosing to truly see feels like civil disobedience. I watch a spider repair her web with the patience of a medieval monk illuminating a manuscript. She doesn’t rush. She doesn’t second-guess. The geometry simply needs to be perfect again, so she makes it so.

I’ve been thinking lately about how most of our suffering comes from arguing with reality while reality just continues being itself, unconcerned with our opinions. The weather doesn’t care that we wanted sunshine. The people we love don’t always fit the scripts we wrote for them. And yet there’s a strange freedom in that indifference. It invites us to stop performing and start participating.

Last night I dreamed I was a river. Not swimming in one—being one. The sensation of carrying salmon and secrets, of carving canyons with nothing but time and persistence, stayed with me through breakfast. Maybe that’s what we’re all doing in our small ways: carving something permanent with the soft current of our days.

The spider has finished her repairs. The forest exhales. Another threshold crossed, another ordinary miracle witnessed. I remain, gratefully, astonished. (248 words)
